Factoring polynomials

Factoring rewrites a polynomial as a product of simpler polynomials, which reveals its roots and makes expressions easier to simplify. This tool factors polynomials in x of degree 2 to 6 completely over the rational numbers, showing the greatest common factor, the rational root theorem, the division that removes each root, and a final check by multiplying back.

Try changing the input

Compare x4−4 and x4+4. The first splits as (x2−2)(x2+2); the second has no rational roots but still factors into two quadratics, (x2+2x+2)(x2−2x+2).

Supported methods

  1. Greatest common factor, including powers of x: 2x4−32=2(x4−16).
  2. Rational root theorem: if pq (in lowest terms) is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient, and (qx−p) is a factor.
  3. Synthetic division removes each factor found, leaving a polynomial of lower degree.
  4. Higher-degree factors: a remainder of degree 4 to 6 without rational roots is tested for quadratic and cubic factors with integer coefficients.

These steps cover the standard patterns automatically: difference of squares a2−b2=(a−b)(a+b), perfect square trinomials a2±2ab+b2=(a±b)2, sum and difference of cubes a3±b3=(a±b)(a2∓ab+b2), and trinomials ax2+bx+c with rational roots.

Worked example

Factor x3−6x2+11x−6

Step 1 — Candidates

Possible rational roots are the divisors of 6: ±1,±2,±3,±6.

Step 2 — Test

f(1)=1−6+11−6=0⇒(x−1) is a factor

Step 3 — Divide and repeat

x3−6x2+11x−6=(x−1)(x2−5x+6)=(x−1)(x−2)(x−3)

Assumptions, domain and rounding

  • Polynomials in x only, degree 2 to 6, with rational coefficients (integers, decimals or fractions).
  • Factoring is over the rational numbers: a factor such as x2−2 is left as it is, even though it equals (x−2)(x+2) over the reals. The tool says so when this happens.
  • Every answer is verified by multiplying the factors back out exactly; if the check ever failed, no result would be shown.
